articles.title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Agentic AI And Infrastructure Are Still On A Roll
articles.description: It was another big week for AI-related startup financings. Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI for R&D, led the pack with a $1 billion series A, followed by Mercor, which secured $750 million to connect AI developers with human experts.
articles.content:
Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

It was another big week for AI-related startup financings. Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI for R&D, led the pack with a $1 billion series A, followed by Mercor, which secured $750 million to connect AI developers with human experts.

Overall, the vast majority of this week’s largest rounds were AI-related, though we did see some biotech, fintech and enterprise software in the mix.

1. Mirendil, $1B, AI for R&D: Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI technology for research and development, secured $1 billion in a Series A funding. Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital led the round for the San Francisco-based startup.

2. Mercor, $750M, human-led AI training: Mercor, a platform that connects AI developers with human experts for model training and evaluation, raised $750 million in Series D funding. The round, backed by a long list of venture investors, set a $20 billion valuation for the San Francisco-based company, which was founded less than four years ago.

3. Torus, $500M, AI infrastructure: Salt Lake City-based Torus, a manufacturer of distributed power and compute infrastructure, announced a $500 million growth financing led by Magnetar Capital. It also introduced a product called Foundry, described as modular AI infrastructure for inference compute.

4. (tied) Path Robotics, $300M, AI for manufacturing: Path Robotics, a developer of physical AI technology for robotics and manufacturing, with initial expertise in welding, picked up $300 million in Series E financing. Georgian led the round, which set a $2.45 billion valuation for the Columbus, Ohio-based company.

4. (tied) LangChain, $300M, agentic AI: LangChain, developer of a platform to run, improve and govern AI agents, closed on $300 million in Series C funding at a $3 billion valuation. CapitalG led the round for the 4-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

6. Nominal, $240M, hardware engineering tools: Nominal, a developer of intelligence tools for hardware engineering, raised $240 million at a $3 billion valuation. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners led the round for the Austin-based startup.

7. (tied) Imprint, $130M, fintech: Imprint, a payments, loyalty and customer intelligence platform for brands, landed $130 million in new funding at a $1.9 billion valuation. Khosla Ventures led the financing for the 6-year-old, New York-based company.

7. (tied) Mavria, $130M, AI infrastructure: Mavria, a startup focused on standardizing how AI infrastructure is developed, built and deployed, launched publicly and said it has raised $130 million in pre-seed and seed funding to date. Its latest round, led by Paradigm, sets a $1 billion valuation for the startup, whose founders formerly worked at the U.S. Department of Energy.

9. (tied) Delix Therapeutics, $100M, biotech: Delix Therapeutics, a startup that says it has “reverse-engineered and optimized psychedelics” to develop treatments for psychiatric and psychological disorders, closed on $100 million in Series C funding. Johnson & Johnson Innovation and SV Health Investors ’ Dementia Discovery Fund led the financing for the Bedford, Massachusetts-based company.

9. (tied) Rox, $100M, sales automation: San Francisco-based Rox, developer of an AI revenue agent for enterprise sales, announced a $100 million Series B financing led by General Catalyst and March Capital.

9. (tied) Databento, $100M, financial market data: Databento, a finance data platform, secured $100 million in Series C funding at a $1.1 billion valuation. Fifth Down Capital led the round for the Salt Lake City-based company.

Methodology

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Nov. 7-13, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

articles.content: At Final Strike Games, Berger met Bradley Boothe, a technical artist and former software engineer who shared a frustration with what could get done at a traditional studio. Together, they struck out on their own, founding the two-person indie studio Freshly Baked Games and trading the security of industry jobs for the creative freedom — and financial uncertainty — of building something entirely theirs. Many years later, the result was a prototype for a game… that was way too ambitious (but they fully intend to return to). So they went back to a different concept, a stripped-down first-person fantasy inspired by FromSoftware's cult-classic King's Field. That was supposed to take a year to build. Three years later, the game, Queen’s Domain, is an ambitious torrent of weaponry, monster encounters, and Berger’s patented 3D level design, all spread across an low-poly open-world map.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering — 10 Most Valuable Star Trek Cards From the New Set
articles.description: These are the 10 most valuable cards in Magic: The Gathering’s Star Trek set, led by Captain Jean-Luc Picard’s $300 Showcase card, Mr. Spock, and Captain Kirk.
articles.content:
Magic: The Gathering’s Star Trek set has been hotly anticipated or controversial, depending on where you stand on the topic of Universes Beyond, but there’s no denying Wizards of the Coast is going all out for it.

With four Commander decks, a Secret Lair drop, and plenty more, there’s a whole bunch for Trekkies to collect. Still, if you’re cracking Collector Boosters (or get really, really lucky with a Play Booster), you may find some of the most valuable cards in the set. Which cards are most valuable? We’ve listed the top 10 below for you.

As ever, pre-release pricing will shift considerably. We’ll be sure to update this list in the coming days once TCGplayer’s data is updated.

The Most Valuable Star Trek Cards In Magic’s Latest Set

10 - Sacred Foundry (Showcase)

Showcase lands are a recurring theme in this list, and this one starts us off at $60.

A Mountain/Plains, the Sacred Foundry taps for red or white mana.

9 - Borg Cube (Showcase)

Up next is the cube-shaped vessel of the Borg. It’s an artifact spacecraft with affinity for artifact creatures, and feeds into the assimilate mechanic, which lets you grab something and turn it into a Borg.

This Showcase Borg Cube variant will set you back $80 at the time of writing.

8 - Overgrown Tomb (Showcase)

Another land on our list, this Swamp/Forest taps for black or green mana and will set you back around $81 right now.

7 - Q, Stacking the Deck (Showcase)

A card with an awful lot of text on it, Q, Stacking the Deck lets you exile cards from the top of your library to exile a nonland card, which in turn lets you create a copy of a card in your hand.

I’m still trying to get my head around it, but the Showcase version is $85 at the time of writing.

6 - Breeding Pool (Showcase)

Another land, Breeding Pool, was seen in Edge of Eternities last year. This Forest Island taps for green or blue mana, and the Showcase version is $92.

5 - Mountain (Surge Foil)

This Legendary crea…. Wait. No, this is a Mountain, just a basic Mountain.

The Surge Foil Mountain, to be precise, is currently selling for over $90. Expect to see this one slide soon, unless I’m missing something.

4 - Dathon, His Heart Open (Showcase)

Looking for a fun Commander for Saga cards? You’ve found one with Dathon, His Heart Open.

Casting an enchantment draws you a card, while Sagas deal two damage to each opponent, plus you can run up the counters on your enchantments - a little like the Counter Blitz precon.

The Showcase version here is $100 at the time of writing.

3 - Captain James T. Kirk (Showcase)

Whether you’re a Kirk or Picard fan, you’re well catered for with this set. Captain James T. Kirk’s Showcase card is going for around $170 ahead of launch weekend.

When it enters or attacks, you can choose one of three options, or go bigger if you have no cards in hand.

2 - Mr. Spock, Science Officer (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

A mono-blue creature that nets players double card advantage was always going to be a big draw (get it?) for players, but adding the inimitable Leonard Nimoy has meant Mr. Spock, Science Officer’s borderless, surge foil version is sitting at around $200.

1 - Captain Jean-Luc Picard (Showcase)

The late, great Patrick Stewart was always going to be on this list somewhere, and the Showcase version of Captain Jean-Luc Picard is sitting at $300, making it the most valuable card in the set.

Picard’s card (heh) gives other creatures +1/+1, and casting a creature or spacecraft gets you a 1/1 Officer token. Get seven of those, and you can search your library for a spacecraft and put it on the battlefield with seven charge counters.

For more of the most valuable Magic cards, be sure to check out our run of the priciest cards from Reality Fracture, The Hobbit, and the most expensive of all time.

articles.title: This Legend of Zelda Triforce Brain Teaser Is Only $13 for Black Friday
articles.description: You can grab this metal Zelda brain teaser puzzle on sale for the lowest price it's ever been, ahead of Black Friday.
articles.content:
The Legend of Zelda games are filled with puzzles for Link to solve. Now there’s a Zelda-themed puzzle for you to solve outside of the games, in real life. It’s a cast metal Triforce, like you’d find in most Zelda games, but it’s a brain teaser. The goal is to figure out how to take it apart, and then figure out how to put it back together. It’s on sale now on Amazon for $12.88, a new all-time low price.

Legend of Zelda Triforce Hanayama Metal Brain Teaser Is 60% Off

The puzzle is made by Hanayama, a Japanese company that specializes in these kinds of brain-teasers. The company actually makes five different Zelda-themed puzzles, but none of the others happen to be on sale at the moment. Hanayama makes a bunch of other non-Zelda-themed puzzles as well, so you can check them out if you like this one.

This Triforce puzzle is comprised of four interlocking metal pieces. Your job is simply to figure out how to slide the pieces around to take them apart. Then, once you have the puzzle disassembled, you can try to re-assemble it.

Hanayama puzzles – or Huzzles, as they're sometimes called – are rated in terms of difficulty, with level 1 being the easiest and level 6 being the hardest. This Triforce puzzle rings in at level 5, so it ought to be pretty tough to figure out. It's aimed at puzzle solvers age 12 and up.

This puzzle, and the other Zelda puzzles that have gone on sale previously, have been incredibly popular with the IGN audience. According to Amazon price tracker Camelcamelcamel, this is the lowest price this puzzle has ever been, and it's by far the cheapest it's been in over a year. It’s unclear when the sale will end, so grab it before the price goes back up.

I’m all about that Hyrule life lately, as I've been playing the Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake and loving every second of it. I’ll probably pick one of these up as a stocking stuffer for the kids.

Keyboards are one of the most important, if not the most important, PC peripherals. You use your keyboard constantly — it's the primary input source for just about everyone (there are a few exceptions). And everyone deserves a keyboard that's a little nicer than the $5 board that was tossed in for free with your last PC purchase. Or — god forbid — whatever's built into your laptop.

If you've got a gamer, a writer, or, well, anyone who uses a computer for any reason in your life, they could probably use a keyboard upgrade. Mechanical keyboards don't usually come cheap, but there are several budget-friendly boards that any keyboard lover would be thrilled to receive. Keyboard accessories under $100

articles.title: The context problem: It’s what’s really breaking AI agents at scale
articles.description: AI models are getting smarter, tokens are getting cheaper, and agents are improving. But the context gap sits between the The post The context problem: It’s what’s really breaking AI agents at scale appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
AI models are getting smarter, tokens are getting cheaper, and agents are improving. But the context gap sits between the modern enterprise and agentic nirvana, keeping many companies from realizing the ROI they hoped for from their AI investments.

As with most problems we’ve seen in the AI era, tech companies are rushing to fill the gap. The New Stack recently spoke with Sri Desikan, an Elastic executive focused on search, to learn more about the AI context gap and how his company is tackling the challenge.

The context gap is easy to understand. As Desikan explains, “frontier models are getting better and better and better,” but if you don’t feed them proper context, “all that money you’re spending on tokens is going to waste.” Getting your agents the information they need, when they need it, quickly, is the ticket to moving from impressive demos to durable automation.

The enterprise is feeling the pinch. AI models can reach out to MCP servers to request information, but merely connecting a company’s corpus to a bridge isn’t enough. You can’t just “shove all this data into [a model’s] context window,” Desikan argues. Why? Because doing so is both computationally expensive (lots of tokens!) and slow.

So what do we need to do? Pre-conform corporate data into an AI index that knows where data is stored and how it relates to other data. Desikan described the process as creating a “container which stores metadata about everything in your enterprise.” Under this formulation, AI agents can access correct, useful information faster and with lower token burn (in some examples, sharply lower ).

There’s another wrinkle worth considering. If you follow Elastic’s guidance and pre-compute your AI context (the index), you can “make sure that stale information” isn’t included, letting companies “know how the LLM is going to think.”

Of course, using AI to pre-prepare data for use by AI agents raises all sorts of privacy and agentic autonomy questions, which I got into with Desikan. Hit play if you want to go deeper on those issues. But looking at the conversation as a whole, I was encouraged by how well-thought-out industry approaches to novel problems seem; nothing that bedevils us today necessarily has to bother us next quarter.

articles.content:
The next map confirmed for Crazy Taxi: World Tour is India, boasting three different zones that celebrate the country’s many cultures and hallmarks — and yes, Bollywood films make an appearance.

Crazy Taxi: World Tour will boast five international maps: the US West Coast, Germany, Japan, Brazil, and finally, India. The India map will feature three distinct zones, labeled City, Countryside, and Industrial.

The City zone is all hustle and bustle, with vibrant marketplaces, nightlife, and architecture. The Country zone is where you can find ancient temples and zoom through the natural landscape, while the Industrial zone takes players on a tour of its trade and commerce hubs, as well as a look at one of the world’s oldest trains.

The game’s official trailer for the India map even teases that players might find themselves on the “set of a Bollywood film,” showing a passenger holding a camera who appears to be a movie director.

This is the latest news to come from this highly-anticipated installment in Sega’s beloved arcade racing game after a closed beta test gave fans a hint at what its multiplayer mode might look like. A signup website for the test says players could participate in two different modes: Pickup Race and Cops ‘N’ Cabbies.

In the Pickup Race mode, up to 6 players compete to drop off as many passengers as possible within a specific time limit and earn as much cash as they can. In Cops ‘N’ Cabbies, two teams of players face off against each other, with one being cabbies and the other being cops hot on their trail.

In addition to multiplayer, the game also has a story mode that follows its main character, Axel, as he chases a gang of international car thieves across the globe to recover his stolen ride, bussing passengers across each country along the way.

We got the chance to preview Crazy Taxi: World Tour back in August. IGN’s Scott White praised the game for its “simple-yet-exciting sort of fun that arcade games excel at, that makes you want to just keep playing,” calling it an “almost refreshingly uncomplicated palette cleanser free of skill trees, crafting systems, and the other chaff that seems to be in every game you play nowadays.”

Crazy Taxi: World Tour launches in early 2027 on Xbox X|S, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and PC.

articles.title: The Lenovo Legion Pro 7i Combines Gaming, Versatility, and Portability in One Premium Package
articles.content:
In our increasingly digital era, what we require from our laptops has expanded exponentially. Gone are the days of only caring about how well they run games and Microsoft Office. Now we also need them for content creation, our jobs, schoolwork, and with a design you can take on the go.

The Lenovo Legion Pro 7i addresses all those needs, providing the versatility and flexibility to shift between tasks seamlessly while also having the power to deliver a high-end gaming experience.

Games Look Beautiful and Run Well

We’re unabashed gamers at IGN, so gaming performance is always going to be a major focus for us with laptops. The Lenovo Legion Pro 7i delivers in that regard, thanks to Intel Core Ultra 9 processors that enable high peak performance. Combined with its full-speed 2.5G ethernet and HDMI 2.1, it performs more like a desktop.

It also has the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 50 Series graphics card, either the 5070, 5080, or 5090. The latter two options provide a full 175W of power, which really unlocks the elite performance of the machine. The gaming experience is completed by a gorgeous 16-inch OLED display with 16:10 aspect ratio, 240 Hz refresh rate, and wide color gamut. It uses Lenovo PureSight to maintain crystal clear image quality and smooth motion. Put simply, if you’re looking for top-of-the-line gaming, this has it.

All of this is supported by the Legion AI Engine+, which dynamically optimizes system performance in real time. It can shift power distribution and balance the loads of the GPU and CPU to optimize the system for the most demanding games, as well as help with heat management. That’s also aided by the Legion ColdFront cooling system, which improves airflow and allows for more efficient heat dissipation to keep performance stable.

Much More Than a Gaming Machine

While gaming is obviously important to us, we recognize that a laptop’s value in 2026 is reliant on it being capable of handling much more than that. Luckily, the Lenovo Legion Pro 7i shines there too.

For the content creators out there, it can easily handle photo and video editing, streaming, graphic design, and professional workloads. The Legion AI Engine+ system also helps with this, since it can tune software to account for what you’re currently working on. That means performance stays strong even during intensive tasks like video rendering or 3D modeling. And its ultra-fast SSD storage means you can quickly switch apps and load files in seconds.

This is all contained within a machine that doesn’t skimp on aesthetics. It has a sleek design made with premium materials and an aluminum finish that gives it a professional look. It won’t look out of place at a coffee shop, but its customizable RGB lighting also gives you options for a little fun.

The Lenovo Legion Pro 7i weighs in at a bit under 6 pounds, so it has some heft to it but is still lightweight enough to be easily transportable. And considering all the bells and whistles it manages to pack in, the weight coming in that low is impressive.

All in all, it proves to be an incredibly powerful machine capable of handling just about anything you throw at it. To learn more about the Lenovo Legion Pro 7i, including all its tech specs and port information, you can check it out on Lenovo’s website. And for more coverage of the best tech out there, stay tuned to IGN.

articles.title: DeepSeek’s coding agent is too tidy for its own good — and benchmarks are punishing it
articles.description: DeepSeek’s open-source coding agent is losing points on a major benchmark for a habit developers usually treat as good practice: The post DeepSeek’s coding agent is too tidy for its own good — and benchmarks are punishing it appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
DeepSeek’s open-source coding agent is losing points on a major benchmark for a habit developers usually treat as good practice: cleaning up after itself.

The problem surfaced when Hugging Face harness optimization researcher Joël Niklaus added DeepSeek Harness to his coding-agent leaderboard, which compares ten harnesses running the same underlying models.

DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth, because one built-in behavior caused it to fail tasks that competing agents completed.

DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth…

“One habit explains much of that gap,” Niklaus writes on X, referring to the agent’s weaker Terminal-Bench performance.

A tidy habit backfires

DeepSeek Harness shuts down background processes when a task finishes, which is a problem for three Terminal-Bench tasks that need those processes to keep running.

Niklaus found that DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, while OpenCode, Pi, and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks.

DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts … while OpenCode, Pi and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks.

That behavior knocked between 1.5 and 1.7 percentage points off DeepSeek Harness’s scores. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at high reasoning effort, it was enough to account for more than the entire 1.3-point gap between DeepSeek Harness and the leader.

The leaderboard’s changelog confirms that the shutdown behavior belongs to DeepSeek Harness itself and the results were left unchanged.

DeepSeek’s engineering documentation describes its local job registry as a deliberately short-lived component. “Choose it when jobs should live in the harness process and die with it,” it states. Jobs that need to survive restarts or run across processes require a different backend.

Same model, different results

Niklaus launched his Harness Leaderboard on November 5 after running 28,849 trials across its original nine harnesses using three open models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Flint.

He kept the model, provider, and reasoning effort constant while swapping harnesses, and the differences were substantial. Mini-swe-agent, a relatively simple bash-based agent, completed 51.4% of tasks compared with 27.3% for OpenClaw, although several other harnesses were statistically tied with the leader.

Costs varied just as dramatically. Pi achieved a 49.4% solve rate at $0.29 per solved task, while OpenCode cost $3.35 per solved task in the initial evaluation. Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf sums up the findings on X as “same open model, different harness => very different results.”

The New Stack contacted DeepSeek for comment on the findings but had not received a response by publication time.

Orchestration isn’t a guarantee

Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan has been running separate evaluations using Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol.

“ Harnesses differed more on cost than on how often they solved tasks,” the researchers write. On multi-user tasks, OpenClaw running Opus 5.5 cost roughly twice as much per solved task as the other Opus harnesses, largely because it repeatedly sent context with each request.

The project also tested Tan’s gstack workflow skills. In 46 sessions, Opus 5.5 read the instructions but never followed the prescribed steps, and the attempts cost roughly twice as much.

The researchers note that the tasks were relatively easy, so it’s unclear whether following the instructions would have improved the results. The results make a case for testing the harness just as carefully as the model.

articles.description: Marvel has confirmed the lineup of heroes that Anthony Mackie's Captain America will lead into battle when Avengers: Doomsday premieres next month.
articles.content:
Marvel has confirmed the lineup of heroes that Anthony Mackie's Captain America will lead into battle when Avengers: Doomsday premieres next month.

Which portion of the big team-up movie's ensemble cast will fall specifically into the Avengers camp was confirmed by Empire. During an interview with some of the movie's cast and crew, the minds behind the Marvel Cinematic Universe talked about what each hero is bringing into the fight and which camp they have ultimately fallen into.

With so many different teams from across the MCU multiverse to keep track of, you may have been a bit confused about who was fighting who and which superpowered being was on whose side. For Mackie, returning as Captain America means leading a new team, and that team now officially encompasses him, Falcon (Danny Ramirez), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Thor (Chris Hemsworth), and Shang-Chi (Simu Liu).

The full team includes faces new and old as Earth's Mightiest Heroes band together to fight off Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom. It'll be far from Mackie's first rodeo as Sam Wilson, but donning the Captain America mantle represents a completely new moment not only for himself but for the characters he's leading. He opened up about the role change during the interview.

"In Endgame, Steve gave him the shield and says, 'You need to be the leader of the Avengers,'" he said. "Now you get to see more of him leading the charge with everyone into battle."

Although we know little about what exactly Doctor Doom's master plan entails, we do know that the primary Avengers team will have some help. Classic X-Men characters and the recently established Fantastic Four will be there to help, too, as will the motley crew of half-heroes known as the New Avengers. The group will almost certainly clash with the classic Avengers lineup, with wild cards like Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) sure to throw a wrench into things, too.

There's… a lot going on in the MCU, but Avengers: Doomsday will give everyone a chance to get their act together. Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige also explained what kind of team viewers can expect.

"We're coming out of years of seemingly no organized Avengers team, and that's exactly when they face these incursions," he said, referencing a post-credits scene from the recently released Avengers: Endgame Encore. "That’s always fun, to put your heroes on the back foot."

Avengers: Doomsday is set to premiere December 18, 2026, meaning we're only a little more than a month away from its release date. Despite there being so little time left, Marvel has shared quite a bit about the project in the lead-up to its launch. Just yesterday, we learned that Deadpool and Wolverine stars Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds have writing credits on the movie. Feige also debunked one of the biggest theories regarding potential connections between Downey's Tony Stark and Doctor Doom.

For more, you can read Mackie's retelling of how he first read that he'd take over as Captain America. You can also watch the commercial that some fans think contains hints about the plot of next month's movie.

If you're an avid PS5 gamer, sooner or later you're going to need more storage. Grand Theft Auto 6, which comes out this month, will take up over 200GB of space alone. That's nearly 25% of your stock 1TB storage space, since a 1TB PS5 drive really equates to less than 850GB of usable storage.

Unfortunately, PlayStation storage deals are practically non-existent in 2026... but that changes today. Ahead of Black Friday, Walmart just dropped the price of the Verbatim Vi7000 1TB PlayStation 5 compatible solid state drive (SSD) to just $129 with free shipping. This is the lowest price I've seen for a high-speed 1TB SSD in months. If you want even more storage, the 2TB model is also on sale for $199. Both models even include a built-in heatsink. Never say never, but I think we'll be hard pressed to find a better price than this during Black Friday proper.

Black Friday Deal: PS5-Compatible 1TB SSD for $129, 2TB for $199

The Verbatim Vi7000 is Playstation 5 compatible. That means it fulfills all of Sony's requirements. It boasts sequential speeds of 7000MB/s read and 6500MB/s write, which easily surpasses the minimum recommended speed of 5,500MB/s. The SSD uses the PCI-Express Gen4x4 interface which slots neatly into the PS5's drive bay. It also has a preinstalled heatsink that will do a fine job of keeping your SSD cool.

The Vi7000 is also a great option as a boot drive for your gaming PC. Surprisingly, this RAM boasts actual DRAM cache. Pretty much every other "budget" SSD at this price point is DRAM-less and relies on HMB, or system memory, as a less expensive alternative. The advantage of having a DRAM cache is faster random read/write performance and faster sustained transfer speeds. It doesn't make much of a difference in a PS5 console but PC users might notice it.

articles.title: 25 Years Ago, Kojima Made the Perfect Metal Gear Solid for the 2020s
articles.description: When Metal Gear Solid 2 launched 25 years ago it seemed almost indecipherable. Today, it's clear that Kojima's sequel was decades ahead of its time, predicting digital disinformation, AI deepfakes, and the breakdown of reality.
articles.content:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Carlos Morales. He’s a long-time fan of the Metal Gear franchise and is an advocate for video games as an artform.

Metal Gear Solid may not be the biggest franchise nowadays, but it was one of the pillars of the first three PlayStation console generations. The adventures of the legendary Solid Snake and his counterparts were not just some of the most critically acclaimed and financially successful games on their respective platforms – they also stand as fantastic and emotional works of art. And what a game Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty is, marking its 25th anniversary this year as somehow having become only more relevant and timely now than it was upon its original release on November 13th, 2001.

Series creator Hideo Kojima may have since moved on to new IPs like Death Stranding and his upcoming espionage action game Physint, but the iconic game director’s narrative idiosyncrasies and uncanny ability to predict how society will develop have rarely felt as fully formed as they do in Metal Gear Solid’s first PlayStation 2 entry. Let’s take a look at why MGS2 was so ahead of its time.

Raiden High

To understand MGS2’s place in contemporary culture, we first have to look at it in a historical context. It may be hard to remember now after so many years of reappraisal, but MGS2 proved somewhat divisive on its initial release. The game received excellent reviews and sold more than seven million copies, but it also attracted controversy for its choice of protagonist and its convoluted storyline. Many fans were upset that most of the game was spent playing as new hero Raiden instead of Snake, and that the game was full of long cutscenes and Codec calls where characters spoke at length about philosophical and sociological issues. In a world that was still getting used to constant internet access becoming more prevalent and was uncertain about what social changes the digital age would bring, MGS2 was a complex game that many in the gaming space, both consumer and professional, didn’t know how to process.

Even IGN’s Ed Lewis said as much in his review of Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater back in 2004, writing that MGS2’s story was of little interest “unless you really want to spend a couple of late, smoky nights going over the details and putting all the pieces together, and they do fit together. While that's kind of interesting if you want a pleasant mind rutting, it was far from fun to watch a game eat itself.”

But time has been kind to MGS2, because many of the topics Kojima explored in the game would become more relevant in the years that followed. The ways social media, the proliferation of digital misinformation for political purposes, and the normalization of automated warfare, deep fakes, and generative AI would turn rifts between demographics into chasms and create a society where many have a tenuous grasp on what reality even is, were all predicted years in advance by Kojima’s landmark title.

Many of the topics Kojima explored in the game would become more relevant in the years that followed. MGS2 is a dense text, and such works can need time to digest. Raiden may have irritated some players in 2001, but he’s now generally accepted as a worthwhile protagonist in his own right by series fans, although it probably doesn’t hurt that Metal Gear Solid 4 turned him into a badass cyborg ninja. People interested in video games as an artform have often pointed to MGS2’s thematic depth, with the game’s story exploring ideas like social engineering, digital censorship, cyberwarfare, and post-truth society. If you just want a tactical espionage adventure with big twists, stealth gameplay, and epic boss fights, the game delivers on those expectations. Yet players embracing MGS2’s more cerebral attributes has made the game an enduring phenomenon even a quarter century later.

One attribute in particular, its metatextual use of game design elements as part of its storytelling, is a big part of why it’s such an impressive artistic achievement.

Game Plays You

MGS2 opens with a prologue featuring series protagonist Solid Snake infiltrating a tanker in the Hudson River to gather evidence of a new Metal Gear prototype named Ray. His ill-fated mission results in the ship sinking, Metal Gear Ray being stolen by recurring villain Revolver Ocelot, and Snake assumed dead. Fast forward two years to a facility called the Big Shell having been built where the tanker sank, which has been taken over by terrorists called Dead Cell and an army of Russian mercenaries under the command of Solidus Snake, one of Snake’s evil clones. They have the President hostage and are seeking to launch a nuclear strike. Raiden, a new agent of FOXHOUND (the same outfit Snake used to work for), is ordered to rescue the hostages and stop the terrorists. Sounds like a standard setup, but it’s not too long into Raiden’s mission that it becomes obvious something is amiss.

Raiden’s mission to the Big Shell has numerous parallels to Snake’s infiltration of Shadow Moses in Metal Gear Solid 1, with repeated plot events, scripted sequences, and character appearances. As the game goes on, the player learns that the entire incident has been orchestrated by a shadow group known as the Patriots, who have covertly controlled the United States government for decades. They’ve also controlled Raiden’s life for years, with his girlfriend Rosemary (who also saves the game for you) being a Patriot agent. The allusions to Shadow Moses are intentional, part of an artificial intelligence simulation system designed to control human behavior and generate desired outcomes. Kojima explicitly makes this plot twist a metaphor for how video game players are conditioned to perform certain actions by subconsciously responding to design choices, with most linear, narrative driven games like the MGS series giving players little to no choice but to do exactly what the developers intend.

Kojima’s metatextual take on the mechanics of game design predates games like BioShock or Spec Ops: The Line. Kojima’s metatextual take on the mechanics of game design predates similar attempts to tie player agency (or lack thereof) into the storytelling of games like BioShock or Spec Ops: The Line. Later levels draw attention to simulational and constructed aspects of video game structure, such as the reveal that the Colonel who Raiden has been taking orders from all game long is one of the Patriots’ AIs, or a big fight on an elevator trying to trick players with a fake Mission Failed screen. Even the environments themselves become less “real” inside the cavernous halls of Arsenal Gear, the flying fortress the terrorists seek to use. The levels have a similar design and color scheme to the VR training missions from the first game, and the room where Raiden battles a fleet of Metal Gear Rays is a surreal space that seems to go on for eternity.

These and other parts of Metal Gear Solid 2 are as interesting to experience now as they were on release. Yet the area where the game is most relevant in 2026 is how it reflects the distorted reality of the mid-2020s.

He Tried To Tell Us

It’s strange to play a video game from 2001 and see it predict the last decade of social upheaval. The gears of late-stage capitalism in the digital age have seen information control and cultural mythology become the most important weapons of the ruling class. In much the same way that the Patriots seek to restrict the free flow of information using the AI system known as GW, so too have the real world military industrial complex and ruling government bodies weaponized social media, digital news distribution, and automated misinformation infrastructure to make it harder to tell what is real or not to suit the interests of the powers that be. The rise of generative AI has done untold damage to the social contract and our ability to believe literally anything we see online, which is not a great development in a world where not using the internet is no longer really an option.

The anonymous nature of the Patriots, who are nameless entities powerful enough to select the President and set the terms of what becomes human history, speaks to how powerless the average person can feel in the face of endless catastrophe. Sure, there are public punching bags among the billionaires, but the movers and shakers of politics and industry are often faceless corporations and private donors who are difficult to directly assign blame to. More than individuals, the system itself is essentially self-perpetuating to the point that it’s daunting to imagine what the world would look like if it were removed. That’s the rationale for President Johnson’s insistence that Raiden continues to battle Solidus even once the Patriots’ deception is exposed, because Solidus’ plan to destroy the Patriots could tip the world into chaos.

Even more distressing is how much of the Patriots’ rhetoric makes sense from a logical standpoint. In a famous speech near the end of the game, the AI Colonel claims that the Patriots don’t censor information for power’s sake, but for the greater good of a society that is becoming directionless under an overwhelming amount of data in the digital era. In the Patriots’ view, “all this junk data preserved in an unfiltered state, growing at an alarming rate” has fractured our grip on collective reality, making it impossible for people to determine what is “true” because the internet rewards polarization and insular thinking with positive reinforcement over objectivity or context. As the Colonel says, “the different cardinal truths neither clash nor mesh. No one is invalidated, but nobody is right.” Check any social media feed or comment section in 2026 and it’s hard to disagree with him.

But MGS2 doesn’t end with the Patriots. It ends with Raiden, a man who has learned everything he’s been programmed to think was a lie, asking what he’s supposed to believe in. Snake tells him to “find the meaning behind the words, then decide. You can find your own name, and your own future.” It’s what makes Raiden’s choice to accept Rosemary back into his life and believe her when she says that she truly did fall in love with him despite being a spy for the Patriots such a fitting resolution. No matter how much the rich and powerful try to determine society’s direction, everyone has the ability to make their own choices and decide what is meaningful to them. It’s a beautiful message that resonates even more today when we’re all trying to survive the turbulent reality we find ourselves in. That Kojima ends a military action game about existentialism by basically telling the player to go touch grass is just another example of why he’s one of the best to ever do it.

Carlos Morales has been writing about sci-fi, superhero movies, and video games since 2019, and has read 10,000 comic books. You can follow his fixations on Twitter.

articles.title: Pokémon Collector Discovers Rare Playable Copy of PokéPark Fishing Rally DS 20 Years After the Limited-Time Event It Was Made For
articles.description: A collector has discovered and authenticated what's believed to be the only surviving, playable copy of PokéPark Fishing Rally, a temporary fishing minigame that was only available to play via wireless download at PokéPark in Japan in 2005.
articles.content:
From May to September 2005, guests at PokéPark — a theme park in Nagoya, Japan centered on Nintendo’s world-famous monster-catching game franchise —could take part in an especially unique, limited-time gaming experience available only for attendees.

This experience was centered around a game called PokéPark Fishing Rally, a fishing minigame that staff wirelessly transferred to guests’ DS handheld consoles via Download Play stations set inside the Park. The game itself was only available on players’ consoles for a 12-hour period after being downloaded, and would erase itself if the DS was powered off. It featured a slew of catchable Water-Type Pokémon, as well as multiple fishing locations and even cameos from non-catchable Pokémon.

Players would compete with other attendees to fish out Pokémon in special events, contests, and organized activities. Surviving photos taken at the Park show that leaderboards were displayed to help competitors keep track of their progress. It’s been twenty years since then, and Nintendo’s unique PokéPark Fishing Rally game had all but faded from the public consciousness… until now.

In July 2026, a player posted an eBay listing for a physical development cartridge of PokéPark Fishing Rally that contained a leaderboard of past attendees’ scores. At first, it was believed to be the only surviving cartridge for this extremely specific title — but now, another collector has come forward with a playable copy of the full game.

Daniel Qudari, an avid collector and Pokémon enthusiast, approached IGN with evidence showing that he is in possession of a functioning PokéPark Fishing Rally cartridge, which is capable of transmitting the game to other DS consoles through Download Play.

To prove that his find was legit and that it actually worked, he sent us exclusive photos and videos showing him running the game on a DS handheld, as well as sending it to other DS consoles that were able to play it. In fact, his discovery was so monumental that he sent it to PSA for authentication, which catalogued and encapsulated the cartridge for posterity.

"I have come across things considered lost media several times in my career. However, this is the first time I have encountered it from a franchise as societally and personally important as Pokémon is. It was an honor and a privilege to experience this game first-hand,” Head of PSA Video Games, Claire Shelton, told IGN in an exclusive statement.

“We are always proud to play a role in documenting, authenticating, and encapsulating unique pieces of video game history such as this. Our involvement allows the item to continue existing and potentially transact with full confidence to any collector, assuring them that this unique piece is assuredly one of the only ways to interact with this formerly lost media piece of Pokémon history."

“PokéPark had some incredible attractions in 2005, and PokéPark: Tsuri Taikai DS, also known as PokéPark Fishing Rally DS, made the experience even more immersive. Fans could catch Pokémon in 3D on their Nintendo DS as they explored the park and entered contests for a chance to win prizes. Imagine being one of those kids and finding out years later that the game you played that day had become a piece of lost Pokémon media,” Qudari said in a separate statement to IGN.

“Pokémon started with video games and grew into a world of manga, trading cards and anime. That’s why preserving a game like this means so much to me. After years of fans wondering if it would ever be playable again, it felt surreal to turn on my DS and spend a quiet moment fishing, then feel that rush when I reeled in a Gyarados. For a moment, I got to feel what it must have been like to play it at PokéPark in 2005.

“What fascinates me is that visitors at PokéPark could download the game wirelessly to their own Nintendo DS back in 2005. With this cartridge in my DS, I can recreate that experience today. I can send the full game directly to someone else’s DS through Download Play, without needing a download station.”

Due to the game’s purposefully temporary nature, and the fact that it was never publicly released or officially distributed, it was generally assumed that nobody would ever get to play PokéPark Fishing Rally again. Qudari did not share exactly how he came into possession of this game, but his discovery is extremely exciting, regardless — and it isn’t the only piece of PokéPark memorabilia he’s collected.

Qudari also shared images and videos of various magazines, brochures, and even merchandise from the PokéPark experience, one of which advertises a Summer Vacation Challenge. In the challenge, the first 200 people to catch a specific ‘target Pokémon’ would earn a special Nintendo DS scratch guard as a prize. A decorative fan was also on offer with advertising for the activity.

If you're so inclined, you can read one woman's firsthand account of her time at PokéPark on her blog, where she recounts her boyfriend's one-in-a-million Shiny Magikarp catch. She even included a photo to commemorate the moment, which, as Qudari puts it, must have felt like "winning the lottery." As most shiny hunters will know, repeatedly restarting your device is a common tactic to increase your chances at snagging a shiny 'mon; given that this game would literally delete itself if that happened, the odds of coming across such a find in such a short amount of time is nothing short of a miracle, and a good example of how special PokéPark was.

This is the latest rare Nintendo find to make headlines after a collector came upon a box of 97 sealed copies of an unreleased version of Super Mario Bros. Duck Hunt earlier this year.

articles.title: Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down
articles.description: If you have one of these AI-generated homepages, you'd better download and save it quick
articles.content:
Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30.

Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names.

Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026."

Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images.

The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of.

It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will.

Mozilla told The Register: "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider."

It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere.

Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now.

Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

articles.title: WoW Forever Has a Weekly Quest That Can Reward Up to 100 Gold, and Players Don't Love It
articles.description: Just a couple days after Blizzard changed the way gold was earned in max-level quests WoW Forever, the company has implemented a weekly quest with loot-box-style gold reward. And players don't love it.
articles.content:
Just a couple days after Blizzard changed the way gold was earned in max-level quests WoW Forever, the company has implemented a weekly quest with loot-box-style gold reward. And players don't love it.

Max level players have found a quest in Booty Bay called 'In Demand - Ancient Elven Curiosities,' which is offered each week, according to Wowhead. There is potential that the quest will rotate to different high level dungeons, but so far, for the two weeks Forever has been out, it's pointed players at Dire Maul, where they have to collect three items. The quest rewards a little bag that can drop one of four items at random that are worth either 10g, 20g, 40g, or 100g.

But while this is a way to get gold in a game where money is scarce, it is rubbing a lot of players in the community the wrong way. For a lot of people, it reminds them of retail WoW, which is built on top of piles and piles of weekly quests to pump additional gold into the economy.

WoW YouTuber Bellular posted the Wowhead link on X / Twitter, captioned simply by "uh what," and followed that up with some criticisms of the new weekly quest. He said: "Retail slop, kill! The way to generate gold is crafting, gathering, selling items. Want to do UBI? Make it sneaky via those means. Don’t show the hand of the designer so clearly." Bellular then tagged Blizzard associate production director Clayton Stone and added: "(pardon the spicy language - some genuine feedback) Let the player earn organically through game systems, not by making content a hoop to jump through."

But it's not just Bellular who's upset at the weekly quest. It's a similar sentiment over on Reddit, where ThatOldGuy7863 simply said: "dear god not weeklys." Meanwhile, drtakhs added: "F**k weeklies and dailies. I’ve been pretty happy with all the decision so far and the thought process behind them was reasonable. Now, what is this? Who wants this? No dailies, no weeklies and no FOMO bulls**t are among the most important things that make classic feel… well like classic…"

However, there may be an explanation for Blizzard's move here. EvadableMoxie suggested a repeatable quest for 100 gold "is aggressively anti-bot."

"It reduces the biggest benefit that bots have, the ability to run 24/7 by frontloading gold rewards," the continued. "This of course does not make bots useless but it reduces their advantage while letting players focus on other things than grinding out gold."

Blizzard has long struggled with bots messing with the economy in every version of World of Warcraft. In the beta, the company had to come down hard on people who were buying and selling gold, which is a direct consequence of botting. Simply put, it's not hard to program a bot to crawl zones for you and gather mining, herbalism or other materials to sell en masse on the auction house. A weekly quest that rewards gold could help players that don't have the time to compete with bots dumping industrial amounts of crafting materials keep up.

But players aren't mad that Blizzard is adding a way to earn gold. Rather, it's the addition of a weekly quest, that encourages players to log on every single week for fear of missing out on an injection of gold. This sort of repeatable quest also wasn't in the original game, with most types of daily and weekly quests not being added until The Burning Crusade.

This is just the latest change as Blizzard tries to nail down the identity of WoW Forever. While there are some parts of the original game that the company has stood firm on, like group tagging, there is an ever growing list of gameplay systems that Blizzard is actively tweaking in Forever, like Dungeon Experience and now, gold rewards.

articles.title: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs
articles.description: Researchers say organizations should have detected and secured them sooner
articles.content:
Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say.

Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump, dated February 2025.

The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise.

However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs.

Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible.

"Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said.

The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session.

Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication.

The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity.

"The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said.

"An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources."

The threats

Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings.

The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger."

Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire.

Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country.

"To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare.

"Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them."

Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats were legitimate.

Hundreds of schools across the Republic of Ireland received the emails, as did news organizations such as RTÉ, which evacuated its Donnybrook campus, disrupting scheduled programming.

Around 300 schools in Northern Ireland received bomb threats, although the PSNI said these were being treated as a hoax, and that the risk to the public was deemed low.

Likewise, Police Scotland confirmed around 1,000 schools were affected by the email campaign and that the threats weren’t believed to be credible.

In France, three school districts confirmed they received similar threats. Separately, domestic and international rail travel, including Eurostar services to London, were interrupted on Thursday following bomb threats made to Calais-Fréthun station.

The latest wave of threats follows similar happenings at other types of organizations in recent weeks, including airline operators, air traffic controllers, and blood banks.

At least 34 flights across various operators in Europe were affected earlier this month. Some were forced into unplanned landings, such as an Aer Lingus flight which pulled up to a French air base instead of its intended target of Rome.

Military fighter jets were also scrambled to escort others in Italian and Austrian airspace. ®

articles.title: Unannounced Intel Core Ultra 7 260K CPU surfaces in Newegg prebuilt gaming PCs
articles.description: The mysterious Intel Core Ultra 7 260K has surfaced in some prebuilt gaming PCs on Newegg, despite no official mention of the chip from Intel.
articles.content:
A new Intel Arrow Lake SKU is listed for sale in multiple prebuilt PCs on Newegg, despite no official acknowledgement of the model from Intel. The Core Ultra 7 260K is a downclocked version of the Core Ultra 7 265K from Intel's main Arrow Lake stack, not the Arrow Lake Refresh stack that's infiltrated our list of the best CPUs for gaming. Outside of a few areas on Newegg's website, you'll find no mention of the CPU elsewhere online (including Intel's official Core Ultra Series 2 specs page ).

Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms

CPU scaling with DLSS

Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape

Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price

AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent

Although retailer-exclusive and late-generation variants are common from AMD and Intel — we recently reviewed the Ryzen 5 5500F, for instance — they almost never fly completely under the radar, as is the case with the Core Ultra 7 260K. The chip itself is identical to the Core Ultra 7 265K based on the specs we know, fitted with 20 cores, eight of which are P-cores. The 260K tops out at 5.4 GHz, however, while the 265K reaches 5.5 GHz.

Otherwise, the specs are all the same. It comes with the same 125W TDP, same 30 MB of L3 cache, and same support for up to 256 GB of memory running at DDR5-6400. We only know of these specs from an image shown on the two ABS prebuilt listings available with the 260K. It's available in the ABS Kaze II paired with an RTX 5060, as well as the Flux II Aqua with an RTX 5070.

The image is below, captured hastily, as you can see, from a Microsoft Teams call. Again, we weren't able to find any information from Intel about the chip outside of this slide.

(Image credit: Intel) One critical detail this slide confirms is that the Core Ultra 7 260K belongs to the Arrow Lake family, not the range of Arrow Lake Refresh processors like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus. It tops out at DDR5-6400, while Arrow Lake Refresh climbs up to DDR5-7200. That means the chip doesn't have access to the hardware-level enhancements available in Arrow Lake Refresh, nor the software-based Intel Binary Optimization Tool that boosts performance in select games.

Although that's enough to categorize the 260K, there are some details that are unclear. In the two PCs it's available in, the chip is referred to as the 260K across the full product page except in Newegg's option selector (pictured below), where it's referred to as the U7-260KF. Intel's KF models are unlocked for overclocking but lack integrated graphics.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Additionally, the slide from Intel referenced above shows the chip boosting up to 5.4 GHz, but the product page lists the chip at 5.2 GHz for maximum boost clock.

Newegg has told us that the chip is exclusive to the retailer and will only be sold through its in-house ABS prebuilts. ABS machines are normally sold with components Newegg already sells piecemeal, offering a convenient way to get a full rig with parts you can identify. The ABS Flux II Aqua, which is available with the chip, is on sale at Newegg now for $300 off.

The ABS Flux II Aqua gaming PC comes with an Intel CPU, an Nvidia GeForce GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, a 1TB NVMe SSD with Gen 4 speeds, and 32GB of DDR5-6000 RAM. This is a 1440p gaming powerhouse with the potential for 4K. View Deal

We've reached out to Intel to get more details about the Core Ultra 7 260K, and we'll update this story when we hear back (see update log above). Although the specs suggest the 260K should perform almost identically to the 265K, we haven't had a chance to test the CPU ourselves. articles.content:
Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.

On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.

Turning a Windows defense against itself

The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

articles.title: Malaysia and Singapore step up Nvidia AI chip probes amidst Jensen Huang controversy
articles.description: Malaysia is investigating possible re-exports of Nvidia AI hardware amid concerns about circumvention of U.S. restrictions on China as Singapore charges an executive over suspicious purchases of 917 AI servers.
articles.content:
Malaysia and Singapore have intensified scrutiny of AI hardware shipments amid concerns about the potential circumvention of U.S. export restrictions on China. Malaysia has launched an investigation into whether AI hardware imported by a subsidiary of the ill-fated Megaspeed was subsequently exported to other countries, reports Reuters. Meanwhile, Singapore has charged another executive over questionable purchases of 917 servers that may contain Nvidia accelerators, according to The Straits Times. The news follows the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over claims he had multiple extra-marital affairs, including with a possible Chinese intelligence asset who facilitated GPU smuggling into China. Analysts speculate that systematic chip smuggling may be the reason behind his departure.

Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs

(Image credit: tsmc) While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market

The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push

Huawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined

China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab

China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained

Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is examining whether Speedmatrix, the Malaysian subsidiary of Singapore-based Megaspeed, re-exported any of the AI processors and servers it had imported for use in local data centers. Apparently, after months of investigating, authorities have yet to find out whether any such shipments occurred and, if they did, whether they complied with Malaysian laws. Malaysia introduced restrictions on the export, transit, and trans-shipment of advanced U.S.-developed AI accelerators in July 2025, so it now requires companies to obtain appropriate permits.

The Malaysian ministry said it was cooperating with customs authorities as well as officials in Singapore and the U.S., and could introduce additional restrictions. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there was no evidence that Megaspeed-related AI hardware had left Malaysia, but he promised to cooperate with international investigations.

Speaking of Megaspeed, the company said on November 12 that it had hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a comprehensive inventory of its AI GPUs and independently assess its compliance with U.S. export-control regulations, reports DigiTimes. The company also confirmed that it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and was prepared to cooperate with other U.S. government agencies if necessary.

James Tan Yong Pong, chief executive of Megaspeed, stressed that compliance with U.S. export rules as well as transparent operations were always a priority for the company. However, Megaspeed did not disclose how many GPUs it owns and which GPU models it has, what BIS examined during its inspections, or whether the authorities had identified any violations.

Meanwhile, Singaporean authorities have brought 41 criminal charges against Shi Bingzhe, a 34-year-old Chinese citizen who served as director of Superphi and chief operating officer of NJ Global Financial. The two companies purchased 917 servers containing restricted Nvidia hardware from Aperia International in 41 transactions between May 2024 and February 2025, according to prosecutors. Authorities allege that the companies had reason to believe the servers were linked to criminal activity by Aperia International. Superphi now faces six charges, while NJ Global Financial faces 35.

The latest charges expand a case that now involves five individuals and six companies. Four firms — Aperia International, A-Speed Infotech, Aperia Cloud Services (II), and Luxuriate Your Life — were charged in July over allegedly making false claims when purchasing servers. Meanwhile, the exact nature of those claims was not disclosed in the report. Authorities have frozen the disposal of a property worth approximately S$55 million and confiscated around S$1 million from bank accounts. Shi faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of S$500,000 per charge if convicted. His next court appearance is scheduled for January 4, 2027.

The two cases largely highlight the significance of Malaysia and Singapore in the supply chain of restricted AI hardware to places where it should not be, such as China. Singapore's investigation focuses on alleged fraud and transactions involving proceeds of criminal activity, whereas Malaysia seeks to find out whether imported AI equipment was subsequently shipped abroad in violation of local regulations.

Neither investigation has found that the hardware ultimately reached China, but both illustrate difficulties that authorities face as they attempt to enforce restrictions on advanced AI hardware across international supply chains.

articles.title: HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing
articles.description: HPE aims for the market with faster, more cost-effective HPC storage to combat rising costs
articles.content:
HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems.

The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack.

The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks.

For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives.

HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads.

One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives, as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported.

HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need.

“When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions.

The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027.

HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control.

Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow.

The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June. ®

articles.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
articles.description: Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII, the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon
articles.content:
NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured this image of the area surrounding the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission in space. Gemini XII was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini Program.

NASA

Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII, the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program.

In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space.

The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way for Landsat, was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.”

For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet.

articles.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond
articles.description: Rivals offer sympathy for stranded admins – and a reminder that putting all your eggs in one basket has consequences
articles.content:
Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study.

Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope.

The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made ), and so on.

At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked.

Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems.

Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register: "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today.

"This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs.

"When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped."

Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure."

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services."

This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as " permanently vulnerable." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal.

And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax."

What a time to be alive. ®
